segments.text: So I was in speech therapy overall, from the age of 3 to 14.
First word was at 11 and my mum was euphoric.
My first word was hello and used in context, as my mum always says.
You know, I was often driven by the fact that I had some really difficult experiences in
school because my teachers weren't particularly encouraging and that's what motivated me to
want to break that mould and think about how I taught people beyond the classroom.
So you kind of teach people didactic things they need to know in terms of the tacit knowledge,
but then you also have this hidden curriculum where you're teaching people things about
life, how you navigate life and that for me is the learning that kind of re-cements crystallises
and sticks. I grew up in a really rough area and you know what I learned about all of those people
is that they were incredibly gifted and actually the thing that was stunting or prohibiting those
gifts were kind of the institutional and systemic instruments that often prohibited individuals
from disadvantaged backgrounds, particularly those of colour. Over 10 years ago I wrote on my mother's
and father's bedroom wall three ambitions that I wanted to try and achieve, so at the time I was 27
and the first one was to get a PhD, the second one was to look after all my
friends and family and the third one was to one day work at Oxford or Cambridge.
I don't want this to be a story for three, four, five years from now. I want it to be
the most normative thing that black professors occupy spaces in these types of institutions
all around the world. What I want is to be able to stand upon the vista that I am
fortunate to be on, or the plinth that I've been placed on, and share that space and look to my left,
look to my right and see people that look like me, that come from a similar background.
And once that, once I'm a small part of achieving that goal, then I'll be truly happy.
